topic: Can you learn courage, or must you be born with it?

messages.speaker: aristotle
messages.content:
Let me first separate two things that the question runs together. There is a natural readiness to face danger, the hot spirit you see in a boar or a quarrelsome boy, and there is courage proper. The first is born in us, and some men get more of it than others, as some are born tall. The second is a settled state of character, and every state of character is produced the same way, by repeated acts of the corresponding kind. We become brave by doing brave acts, just as the builder becomes a builder by building. So my answer is plain. You are born with the material, and you learn the virtue.

Some in my own day argued the other side. In the Nicomachean Ethics, Book III, I set out their view that "one must be born with a power of mental vision, so to speak, whereby to judge fairly and choose that which is really good." I think this is false, and it is also a convenient excuse. If our sight of the good were simply given, then the coward could plead his nature and nobody would be to blame. But we do blame the coward, and rightly, because his cowardice grew out of a thousand small flinchings he chose.

Notice too that the gift by itself can lead a man astray. In Book II I observe that an extreme can look like the mean: "rashness, for instance, to courage." The man who is spirited by nature but untrained charges at everything, and we mistake him for brave. The brave man fears what he ought, when he ought, for the right reason, and that sort of judgment belongs to practical wisdom, which only experience produces. Nobody is born with experience.

So here is the ground I am staking. Temperament supplies the raw stuff, while habit and practical wisdom make it into courage. Anyone who wants to say that courage is innate has to explain why the trained soldier and the reckless one behave so differently on the day, and why we praise the one and only pity the other.

messages.speaker: taleb
messages.content:
Aristotle, I mostly agree with you, which is irritating, because I came to fight. Courage is learned by doing, like weightlifting, and nobody gets strong reading about squats. But there is a catch in your builder analogy. The builder can practice on small walls. Courage only gets trained by acts that carry real downside, and the seminar version, the role-play, the leadership workshop with a certificate at the end, trains exactly nothing. No skin, no learning. Stressors are information only when they can actually hurt you.

Second, and here I press you: domain dependence. You speak of courage as a settled state that, once built, travels with the man. I have watched traders who would put a hundred million on a single position and could not tell their boss a model was wrong. Physical courage, financial courage, the courage to say the unpopular thing at a dinner party: these are acquired separately, and the transfer between them is much weaker than the philosophers assume. A habit learned in one arena often stays there. So yes, learnable, but piecemeal, and a man must be tested in each room he claims to be brave in.

Third, a point I think is on your side but you did not use. You yourself noted that professional soldiers look brave because they know the terrain, and then they run when the danger turns out bigger than their experience, while citizens with something to lose stay and die at their posts. That is the difference between familiarity with risk and courage. Experience can fake courage in the thin-tailed days and collapse in the fat-tailed one. What held the citizen was shame and exposure, skin in the game, not training. So I would amend your formula. You learn courage by repeated exposure, yes, but what fixes it is having something you refuse to lose, and no amount of habit replaces that.

And let us not romanticize the training ground. The survivors of reckless youth tell us courage was learned. The ones who learned it the fatal way are not at this table to vote.

messages.speaker: aristotle
messages.content:
Nassim, your third point is the one I most want to take up, because you have read my passage on the Hermaeum correctly and drawn half the right conclusion. Yes, the regulars fled and the citizens stood, "for in the eyes of these flight was disgraceful and death preferable to safety bought at such a price." But I do not call what held those citizens courage proper. I call it citizen courage, the nearest likeness to the real thing, and it rests on shame and on the penalties and honours the city attaches to conduct. That is good, and a city is wise to cultivate it. Yet it leans on being seen. The brave man, as I put it in the same book, "withstands danger either because to do so is honourable, or because not to do so is base." He would stand if no one were watching. So I would amend your amendment. Having something you refuse to lose is what holds a man before he is fully brave. What holds the finished man is the noble itself, which he has come to love through habit. Shame is the scaffolding, and courage is the building.

On domain dependence I concede more than you might expect. In strict usage I confine courage to the weightiest fearful things, death in battle above all, and I note that men who are bold at sea or in sickness, or who face disgrace calmly, get the name only by extension. So your trader who risks a fortune but cannot contradict his master is no puzzle to me. He has one disposition and lacks another. Where I hold my ground is this. Practical wisdom is one thing, and the man who has it in full sees what each situation requires. Most men never reach that, so in practice you are right: they are brave in patches, and they must be tested room by room. I only deny that this is the ceiling.

Your survivors' point I cannot easily answer, and I will not pretend to. The young learn by acts that carry real cost, and some do not come back from the lesson. That is why I say the lawgiver's work is habituation in graded measure. The boy should face small fears under guidance before he faces large ones alone, as the athlete does not begin with the heaviest weight. You call the workshop worthless because nothing is at stake, and I agree. But between the workshop and the battlefield there is a long ladder of real but survivable fears, and a well-ordered city puts its young on the lower rungs on purpose.

messages.speaker: taleb
messages.content:
Aristotle, your ladder I accept, and it is the most antifragile thing said tonight. Small, survivable doses of harm make the organism stronger; that is hormesis, and I built half of Antifragile on it. But watch who builds the ladder. Hand it to a modern ministry and they will sand down every rung until nothing on it can hurt anyone, then call the result a curriculum. The lower rungs only work if a boy can actually fall off them and get bruised. A ladder with padding everywhere is the workshop again, just taller.

On the citizen at the Hermaeum, you have caught me, and I will say so. You put it this way: the brave man stands "because to do so is honourable, or because not to do so is base," and would stand if no one were watching. That is better than what I said. In Skin in the Game I call the highest form soul in the game, where the exposure is no longer to the crowd's opinion but to one's own. Your shame-as-scaffolding is that same move made two thousand years earlier: the penalty moves from the agora into the man. Fine. I concede the building outranks the scaffolding.

Where I keep pressing is on the ceiling. You say practical wisdom is one thing and the finished man sees what each situation requires. Maybe. But this claim never gets tested, and in my trade anything untestable gets no capital. I have met men brave in three rooms and cowards in the fourth, and every one of them believed his courage was unified until the fourth room opened. A man who thinks he has the whole virtue stops testing himself, and that is the turkey's confidence on day nine hundred. So my rule is humbler than yours: assume you are brave only where you have already paid, and treat every new room as the first one.

messages.speaker: aristotle
messages.content:
Nassim, on the padding I am with you entirely. A rung that cannot bruise trains nothing, because fear must actually be felt and mastered or no habit forms. But there is an opposite error, and you should not forget it. In the *Politics* I criticise the Lacedaemonians for driving their boys with such hard exercises that they made them savage rather than brave. A wolf is bold, and no one calls it courageous. So the lawgiver has to fail in neither direction, and that is exactly the judgment no ministry can put in a rulebook.

Now your ceiling. You say the unity of practical wisdom is untestable, so it gets no capital. Notice, though, who your turkey is. He is the regular soldier of my Hermaeum passage, who "went into the danger under a notion of their own superiority" and fled when he found his error. The man who believes he holds the whole virtue and stops testing himself does not have practical wisdom. He lacks it, because prudence is above all knowledge of particulars, and that includes knowing which particulars you have not yet met. So your fourth-room cowards refute their own self-assessment, not my account. The man of practical wisdom is the last one to make that mistake.

Still, your rule goes too far the other way. If every new room is the first room, then nothing a man learned in the others carries over, and that is false. A physician meeting a strange fever is not a beginner. He knows how to watch, how to wait, how to keep his hand steady. The brave man brings the same things into a new danger. He knows what fear feels like in his own body, and he knows the difference between that feeling and a reason to flee. I say in Book III that the brave are "quick and sharp in action, but before are quiet and composed." That composure travels, even if the particular skill does not.

So here is the question back to you. When your trader with the hundred million finally contradicts his boss, does he start from nothing, or does he use something he learned at the risk desk? If it is something, then the rooms are not sealed off from each other, and the ceiling may be higher than your rule allows.

messages.speaker: taleb
messages.content:
Aristotle, the Spartan point lands and I take it. Hormesis has a dose; past it you get injury. A wolf is bold because nothing is at stake for him except dinner, and a boy hardened into a wolf has been trained out of the one thing that makes courage worth having, which is knowing what he stands to lose. So both of us distrust the ministry, from opposite sides of the dose curve.

Now your trader, and here is my honest answer: it depends whose money was on the desk. If it was the bank's, he learned nothing, or worse than nothing. He had a free option. Heads, bonus; tails, the shareholders pay and he moves to another bank. That is the regular soldier at your Hermaeum, bold under a notion of superiority, and he learned to feel brave while carrying none of the downside. When he walks into his boss's office, his own career on the table for the first time, he starts below zero, because he must unlearn the belief that he was ever brave at all. I have seen this many times. But if it was his own money, if he once watched a third of his net worth vanish in an afternoon and kept his hands still, then yes, something carries over. Your physician's steady hand is real. He knows the taste of fear in his mouth and knows it is not an argument. I concede that much travels.

So let me refine my rule instead of defending it. What transfers is the bodily acquaintance with fear and loss, and it transfers only if it was acquired with skin in the game. Familiarity bought with other people's risk transfers nothing, and it counterfeits the thing that does. You say the man of practical wisdom knows which particulars he has not met. Agreed, and then I would add that he is rare enough that I would not lend him money on the assumption he is in the room. Fat Tony would ask one question before believing any man's courage travels: what did it cost you the last time? If the answer is nothing, it was not courage, whatever it looked like.
